title: Edge Detection: R_TRIG, F_TRIG and One-Scan Pulses
oneLiner: Levels vs edges: why a held button is TRUE for hundreds of scans, how R_TRIG and F_TRIG turn a change into a pulse that lasts exactly one scan, and the ladder and hand-written equivalents.
keyTakeaway: Act on levels for things that should last as long as a signal does, and on edges for things that should happen once per event. R_TRIG gives one scan of TRUE when its input rises; give each signal its own instance and call it every scan.
explanation:
Most PLC inputs are levels: a button is TRUE for as long as it's held, which at a 10 ms scan is dozens or hundreds of scans. Some actions should happen once per event instead: count a part, toggle a light, add one to a total, start a sequence. For those the program needs the edge, the moment the signal changes, not its level.

A rising edge is a change from FALSE to TRUE, and a falling edge a change from TRUE to FALSE. IEC 61131-3 provides two function blocks for detecting them: R_TRIG, whose output Q is TRUE for exactly one scan after its input CLK rises, and F_TRIG, which does the same when CLK falls. Inside, each just remembers last scan's value of CLK and compares. A signal that is TRUE for exactly one scan like this is called a one-shot or one-scan pulse.

Ladder has the same thing as transition contacts that pass power for one scan, and you can write it by hand in two lines of ST. Hold the button down in the simulator below to see the difference between counting a level and counting edges.
